name: Guihua Jiu
description: Osmanthus blossom steeped in rice wine — intensely floral, apricot-scented, and traditionally opened at the Mid-Autumn Festival.
funFact: Guilin is named for its osmanthus forests — 'gui' is the flower, 'lin' the forest — and the wine is drunk at the Mid-Autumn Festival when the trees are in bloom.

steps: Rinse the dried osmanthus blossoms briefly and let them dry.
Layer them with rock sugar in a clean glass jar.
Pour over the rice wine and seal.
Store somewhere dark for at least one month, longer for a stronger infusion.
Strain and serve in small cups, lightly chilled or at room temperature.

name: Warm Huangjiu
description: Shaoxing rice wine warmed with ginger and dried plum. Nutty, savoury and closer to a dry sherry than to anything in the wine aisle.
glassware: Small ceramic cup and warming pot
funFact: Huangjiu has been brewed in Shaoxing for over two thousand years, and warming it is not just for comfort — heat volatilises the harsher notes and brings the amino-acid savouriness forward.

steps: Pour the huangjiu into a small ceramic warming pot.
Add the ginger slices, dried plum and rock sugar.
Stand the pot in a bowl of hot water — never over direct heat — until it reaches about 40°C.
Pour into small cups and drink while warm, alongside food.

name: Old Monk and Cola
description: India's dark vanilla-heavy rum with cola and lime. Sold on nostalgia and almost no advertising, and ordered in every Indian bar regardless.
funFact: Old Monk has barely advertised since it launched in 1954 and still sells on word of mouth alone — for decades it was among the largest-selling dark rums in the world.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the rum and the lime juice.
Top with cold cola.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Urrak with Limca
description: The first distillation of cashew feni, cut with lemon soda, salt and a green chilli. Goa's summer drink, available for about three months a year.
funFact: Urrak only exists during the cashew season from March to May — it is feni stopped after the first distillation, and it cannot be stored, so Goans drink the whole supply in a single summer.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice and add the pinch of salt.
Pour in the urrak and the lime juice.
Top with cold Limca.
Drop in a slit green chilli and stir once.
Drink cold, in the shade.

name: Arak Madu
description: Balinese palm arak with honey and lime, over ice. Simple, floral and everywhere on the island once the sun goes down.
funFact: Balinese arak is distilled from palm sap or rice and is used in Hindu ceremony as well as at the beach bar — the ritual pouring of arak onto the ground precedes many temple offerings.

steps: Loosen the honey with a splash of warm water so it will mix.
Shake the arak, honey syrup and lime juice hard with ice.
Strain into a tumbler over fresh ice.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Bamboo
description: Dry sherry and dry vermouth, stirred cold with bitters. Low-proof, saline and quietly elegant — and one of the first great cocktails invented in Asia.
funFact: Created by Louis Eppinger at the Grand Hotel in Yokohama in the 1890s — decades before Japan's cocktail culture became famous, and still the best argument for sherry in a mixing glass.

steps: Combine the sherry, vermouth and both bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds — this drink is low-proof, so watch the dilution.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Lemon Sour
description: Shochu, soda and a whole lemon's worth of juice. Japan's izakaya default — and in Tokyo you often squeeze it yourself, at the table.
funFact: Some Tokyo izakayas serve a 'denki bran' style tabletop version with a frozen lemon half and a hand press, and others install taps that dispense the shochu-soda base directly.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice — the colder the better.
Add the shochu and the fresh lemon juice.
Top with well-chilled soda water.
Stir once, vertically, to preserve the carbonation.
Garnish with a lemon wheel or a squeezed half.

name: Million Dollar
description: Gin, vermouth, pineapple and egg white shaken to a thick foam. Eppinger's other Yokohama invention, and the one Somerset Maugham wrote about.
funFact: Maugham name-checked it in his Malayan stories, and the Raffles Hotel in Singapore served it long enough that both cities now claim it.

steps: Dry-shake all the ingredients without ice for 15 seconds to build the foam.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Grate a little nutmeg over the foam.

name: Umeshu Soda
description: Japanese plum liqueur lengthened with soda over ice. Sweet-tart, almond-scented, and the easiest drink in any Japanese fridge.
funFact: Umeshu is made by steeping unripe ume — closer to an apricot than a plum — in shochu with rock sugar; families still make it each June and the stone gives it a faint marzipan note.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the umeshu.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once gently and drop in a preserved ume if you have one.

name: Airag
description: Fermented mare's milk, sour and lightly effervescent. The drink of the steppe, offered to every guest who enters a ger.
funFact: Refusing the bowl outright is a serious discourtesy in Mongolia; the accepted compromise is to touch it to your lips and return it, which satisfies the custom.

ingredients.item: A leather khokhuur bag or wooden churn

steps: Pour the fresh mare's milk into the khokhuur with a cup of the previous batch as starter.
Churn it repeatedly throughout the day — traditionally a thousand strokes or more.
Let it ferment for one to three days, continuing to churn.
Taste until it is sour, faintly fizzy and lightly alcoholic.
Serve cool in a wide bowl, offered with the right hand.

name: Tongba
description: Fermented millet in a wooden pot, topped with hot water and sipped through a bamboo straw. Refill the water and keep going until it stops tasting of anything.
glassware: Wooden tongba pot with a bamboo straw
funFact: It belongs to the Limbu people of eastern Nepal, and the etiquette is specific: you top up the same millet with hot water several times, and it is impolite to stop after one.

ingredients.item: A wooden tongba pot and bamboo straw (pipsing)

steps: Pack the fermented millet into the wooden tongba pot.
Pour in hot — not boiling — water to cover.
Let it steep for about five minutes.
Sip through the perforated bamboo straw, which filters out the grain.
Top up with more hot water two or three times as you drink.

name: Gin Pom
description: Ginebra San Miguel with powdered pomelo juice and ice. Cheap, sharp and the most-drunk gin serve in the world's biggest gin market.
funFact: The Philippines drinks more gin than any other country on earth, almost all of it Ginebra San Miguel — and most of that is mixed with a sachet of powdered juice costing a few pesos.

steps: Dissolve the powdered drink mix in the cold water in a pitcher.
Add the gin and stir well.
Pour over ice into tall glasses.
Serve with a calamansi wedge if you have one.

name: Weng Weng
description: Every white spirit on the shelf plus whisky, orange juice and grenadine. Named for the noise your head makes afterwards.
funFact: 'Weng weng' is Filipino for dizzy or spinning; the drink is a Boracay beach-bar institution, and most bars cap the order at two per person.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add all five spirits.
Top with orange juice and stir.
Pour the grenadine down the inside of the glass so it sinks to the bottom.
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry.

name: Makgeolli
description: Unfiltered rice brew, milky and lightly fizzing, poured from the bottle into a shallow bowl. Korea's oldest drink and its most farmhouse.
funFact: Nuruk — a wild-yeast and mould starter cake — does the work that malting does for beer, breaking down the rice starch; makgeolli is traditionally drunk after farm work, and increasingly after rain, by tradition.

steps: Steam the rice and cool it to room temperature.
Mix the rice with the crumbled nuruk and the water in a clean crock.
Cover with cloth and ferment at room temperature for about a week, stirring daily.
Strain through cloth, pressing lightly — makgeolli is meant to stay cloudy.
Refrigerate, and shake the bottle before pouring into shallow bowls.

name: Somaek
description: Soju dropped into beer, in a ratio people argue about seriously. Korea's most-poured mixed drink, and the engine of the company dinner.
glassware: Beer glass and a soju shot glass
funFact: The golden ratio is contested — three parts beer to one soju is the common baseline, and there are Korean drinking games devoted entirely to pouring it correctly.

steps: Pour the beer into a glass, leaving room at the top.
Add the soju — either poured in or dropped in the shot glass whole.
Cover the top with your palm and tap the glass once on the table to mix it.
Drink promptly, while it is still fizzing.

name: Yogurt Soju
description: Soju, Yakult and lemon-lime soda. Tastes like a children's drink, disappears like one, and is not one.
funFact: Yakult has been sold in Korea since 1971 and is delivered door to door by the 'Yakult ajumma'; the cocktail is the reason Korean convenience stores stock it next to the soju.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the soju and the Yakult.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Stir once and serve immediately — it separates if it sits.

name: Arrack and Ginger Beer
description: Ceylon coconut arrack with ginger beer and lime — the island's standing highball, and better than it has any right to be.
funFact: Ceylon arrack is distilled from fermented coconut flower sap, tapped by climbers who move between palm crowns on ropes — a job with its own hereditary caste of specialists.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the arrack and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Boba Cocktail
description: Milk tea, rum and tapioca pearls in a shaker. Taipei's bars took the island's most famous export and put a wide straw in it.
glassware: Tall glass with a wide straw
funFact: Bubble tea was invented in Taichung in the 1980s; Taipei's cocktail bars started spiking it in the 2010s, and the brown-sugar version is now a fixture across East Asian bar menus.

steps: Cook the tapioca pearls and toss them in a little brown sugar syrup while still warm.
Spoon the pearls into the bottom of a tall glass.
Shake the rum, cooled tea, milk and remaining syrup hard with ice.
Strain over the pearls and add fresh ice.
Serve with a wide boba straw.
recipe.garnish: Brown sugar syrup streaked down the glass

name: Thai Bucket
description: Thai rum, Red Bull and cola in a child's sand bucket with several straws. Structurally a punch, spiritually a warning.
funFact: Thai Red Bull — Krating Daeng — is uncarbonated, sweeter and more heavily caffeinated than the export version, which is a meaningful part of why the buckets have the reputation they do.

steps: Fill a small plastic bucket with ice.
Pour in the half-bottle of Sangsom.
Add the bottle of Thai Red Bull.
Top with cola and stir with a straw.
Share it — the bucket is designed for four straws, not one.

name: Rượu Rắn
description: Rice wine with a snake in the bottle. Sold as a tonic, drunk as a dare, and genuinely traditional across northern Vietnam.
funFact: The ethanol denatures the venom, which is why the practice is not as dangerous as it looks — though the bottles are still confiscated at most international borders.

steps: Clean and prepare the snake thoroughly — this step is traditionally done by a specialist.
Place it in a large sealed glass jar with the herbs and ginseng.
Cover completely with rice wine and seal airtight.
Leave to infuse for several months to a year.
Serve in very small cups, at room temperature.
